text: Name a text data augmentation technique
note: Any way to create extra or perturbed training text or text pairs: rules, noise, mixing, translation, generation, counterfactual edits. Not image-only tricks.

answers.q: Translate to French, translate back, enjoy the reworded sentence. Sennrich's 2016 MT trick, now everywhere.
Swap words for WordNet synonyms. Fast, rule-based, and occasionally hilarious.
Drop each word with probability p. Costs nothing and teaches the model not to lean on any single word.
Insert a synonym of a random word at a random position.
Pick two words and swap their positions, n times.
Same meaning, different words. Done by rules, seq2seq models or, these days, by prompting an LLM.

aka: Easy Data Augmentation Techniques for Boosting Performance on Text Classification Tasks
answers.q: Wei and Zou 2019: synonym replacement, insertion, swap and deletion in one package. No models needed; still the baseline for small datasets.

aka: Augmenting Data with Mixup for Sentence Classification
answers.q: Blend two examples and their labels. Pixels are easy; for text you interpolate embeddings or hidden states, not words.

aka: AEDA: An Easier Data Augmentation Technique for Text Classification
answers.q: Karimi et al. 2021: sprinkle random punctuation marks between the words. Every token stays, in order. Beat EDA on five datasets.
Replace a word with a neighbour in word2vec or GloVe space. Wang and Yang 2015 did it for tweets.
Mask a word and let BERT refill it. The replacement fits the sentence, unlike a thesaurus lookup.
Randomly insert, delete, substitute or swap characters. Cheap insurance against typos.

aka: prompting an LLM to generate examples
answers.q: Prompt a strong model to write new labelled examples. Quantity is free; diversity and label noise are the catch.
Replace random tokens with a [MASK] or [UNK] placeholder, so the model learns from the context around them.

aka: Unsupervised Data Augmentation for Consistency Training
answers.q: Xie et al.: consistency training. Make predictions on a sentence and its back-translation agree, using unlabeled data.
Flip a sensitive attribute, such as he to she, and keep the label. A standard bias-mitigation trick.

aka: Cutoff: A Simple but Tough-to-beat Data Augmentation
answers.q: Zero out a whole token, a feature dimension or a span of the embedding matrix. Image Cutout's cousin for NLP.
Fill slots in hand-written templates with lists of entities. Dull, but great for intent classifiers.
Typos that a real finger would make: 'p' becomes 'o', never 'z'.
Prefix every synthetic back-translated sentence with a special tag so the model knows it isn't real.
Machine-translate English training data into the target language and train on that. A hard-to-beat cross-lingual baseline.
Randomly replace words with their translations into other languages, so that one sentence mixes several.

aka: MixText: Linguistically-Informed Interpolation of Hidden Space for Semi-Supervised Text Classification
answers.q: TMix interpolates the hidden states of two texts at a chosen layer. Chen et al. 2020.
Keep a random contiguous chunk of the text. The text-world cousin of random crop.
Edunov et al. 2018: back-translate by sampling or noised beam search, not plain beam, so the synthetic source is more varied.

aka: SwitchOut: an efficient data augmentation algorithm for neural machine translation
answers.q: Wang et al. 2018: randomly swaps words in both the source and the target sentence for translation models.

aka: Soft Contextual Data Augmentation for Neural Machine Translation
answers.q: Replace a word's embedding with a probability-weighted mixture of its likely substitutes, rather than committing to one.
Şahin and Steedman 2018: crop a sentence down to a subtree, or rotate subtrees around the head. For low-resource languages.
Corrupt a sentence, then have BERT reconstruct it: samples near the data manifold, with the label carried over.

aka: Do not have enough data? Deep learning to the rescue
answers.q: Fine-tune GPT-2 on labelled examples, generate new ones per class, and keep those a classifier agrees with. Not the LAMBADA dataset.

aka: GPT3Mix: Leveraging Large-scale Language Models for Text Augmentation
answers.q: Show GPT-3 a mix of real examples, have it write new ones, and train on its soft labels. Yoo et al. 2021.

aka: Generative Data Augmentation for Commonsense Reasoning
answers.q: Yang et al. 2020: generate synthetic commonsense QA examples with GPT-2, then filter for informativeness and diversity.

aka: Augmented SBERT: Data Augmentation Method for Improving Bi-Encoders
answers.q: A slow cross-encoder labels new sentence pairs, which then train the fast bi-encoder.

aka: Data Diversification: A Simple Strategy For Neural Machine Translation
answers.q: Train forward and backward translation models, then add all of their predictions to the training data.
Singh et al. 2019: replace a segment of the input with its translation into another language.
Swap a keyword for its WordNet hypernym: "dog" becomes "animal". From GenAug.
Swap content words for random ones of the same part of speech: grammatical but meaningless. Colourless green ideas, as a dataset.
NER augmentation: swap an entity mention for another mention of the same type from the training set.
Dai and Adel 2020: replace each token with another token that has the same tag, drawn from the training set.
NER augmentation: split a sentence into segments, then shuffle the words inside each one, leaving the tags attached.

aka: Data Recombination for Neural Semantic Parsing
answers.q: Jia and Liang 2016: induce a synchronous grammar from the training pairs, then sample new pairs from it.
Andreas 2020: if two fragments appear in the same context somewhere, swap them in every other context too.

aka: Substructure Substitution: Structured Data Augmentation for NLP
Data Augmentation with a Generation Approach
Data Augmentation with a Generation Approach for Low-resource Tagging Tasks
answers.q: Linearise tagged sentences, train a language model on them, then sample brand-new labelled sequences.

aka: SeqMix: Augmenting Active Sequence Labeling via Sequence Mixup
SSMix: Saliency-Based Span Mixup for Text Classification
answers.q: Mix text by pasting in the other sentence's most salient span, so the mixed input is still real text.

aka: Nonlinear Mixup: Out-Of-Manifold Data Augmentation for Text Classification

answers.q: Interpolate hidden states at a random layer instead of the raw input.

aka: Learning the Difference that Makes a Difference with Counterfactually-Augmented Data
answers.q: Kaushik et al.: people minimally edit each review so its label flips, forcing models to learn what actually matters.
Swap he and she, king and queen, and so on, to balance gendered associations. Zhao et al. 2018 for coreference.

aka: Adversarial Example Generation with Syntactically Controlled Paraphrase Networks
answers.q: Iyyer et al. 2018: paraphrase a sentence to match a target syntactic template, say active voice into passive.

aka: Data Noising as Smoothing in Neural Network Language Models
answers.q: Xie et al. 2017: replace random words with a blank, or with a draw from the unigram distribution, as smoothing for neural LMs.
SimCSE's trick: encode the same sentence twice with different dropout masks and call them a positive pair. No edits at all.

aka: Adversarial Examples for Evaluating Reading Comprehension Systems
answers.q: Jia and Liang 2017: append a misleading but irrelevant sentence to the passage. Train on it, and QA models stop being fooled.

aka: Data Augmentation for Low-Resource Neural Machine Translation
answers.q: Fadaee et al. 2017: synthesise new contexts for rare words by swapping them into places where a frequent word was predicted.
Interpolate between minority-class examples to rebalance a dataset. For text, the interpolation happens on embeddings or feature vectors.
Swap characters the way a scanner does: l for 1, rn for m, O for 0.

aka: Self-Instruct: Aligning Language Models with Self-Generated Instructions
Unnatural Instructions: Tuning Language Models with (Almost) No Human Labor
